risk.detail: Greenhouse reviews partner applications on the first Monday of each month and needs a mutual customer, so a missed cycle adds weeks.
risk.mitigation: Apply before the next first Monday with this customer as the mutual customer, and launch read-only or with staff confirming until approval.

systems.name: Lever
systems.access: Lever REST API. Partner integrations must use OAuth 2.0; Lever gives partners no API keys. A customer-made API key over Basic auth is the legacy path and needs the customer’s Data API feature.
systems.sandbox: A partner sandbox API and an integrator sandbox account.
systems.limits: 10 requests per second per key, with bursts to 20, and 429 past that. Lever says these defaults aren’t guaranteed.
blockers: Production credentials come after Lever’s review: a help-center article, two review logins and a QA walkthrough.
Only a Super Admin can authorize the app.
Access to confidential postings and requisitions is granted when the credential is created and can’t be added later.
EEO responses have their own scopes, and the Candidates endpoints are deprecated in favor of Opportunities.
systems.request: OAuth approval from a Super Admin, the scopes the workflow needs (including confidential data, if any), and the postings and stages in scope.
systems.check: Opportunities, notes and stage changes land on the right posting, with no duplicate contacts.

risk.title: Confidential roles stay hidden from the agent
risk.detail: Lever grants access to confidential postings only when the credential is created, so if it’s missed, those roles stay hidden until a new credential is issued.
risk.mitigation: Ask whether any roles in scope are confidential before the Super Admin authorizes, and include a confidential posting in replay.

systems.name: Workday Recruiting
systems.access: The customer’s admin creates an Integration System User (ISU) and registers an API client in their own tenant. Recruiting runs on SOAP web services (Get_Candidates, Put_Candidate, Get_Job_Requisitions and more); REST uses OAuth 2.0 with the ISU’s refresh token. Workday also documents agent-to-agent (A2A) and MCP connections for external agents.
systems.sandbox: Customer sandbox tenants. Confirm the refresh schedule with the customer; reports say they refresh weekly from production.
systems.limits: Per-endpoint caps aren’t published. Under load, REST returns 429 and SOAP returns 500, and Workday may throttle or suspend access past its limits.
blockers: The ISU needs domain security policies in an integration system security group, and the policy change must be activated.
Registering the API client needs a security administrator.
Some Recruiting operations have preconditions; for example, a new job requisition needs a position with no open requisition.
Workday’s partner program is optional and paid. Confirm the price with Workday; one integration guide puts it at $15,000 a year.
systems.request: An ISU with only the Recruiting domains the workflow needs, a registered API client, a sandbox tenant, and a named Workday security admin.
systems.check: Candidates and job applications land on the right requisition and stage in the sandbox tenant.

risk.title: Workday security setup waits on the customer’s admin
risk.detail: Every permission the agent needs is a domain security policy that the customer’s Workday security admin must grant and activate.
risk.mitigation: Send the exact domains and operations with the access request on day 1, and test them in the sandbox tenant before production.

systems.name: Ashby
systems.access: Ashby API (RPC-style POST calls with JSON). An organization admin creates an API key, used as the Basic auth username, and can tag it to an integration partner.
systems.sandbox: Not documented. Confirm with Ashby.
systems.limits: 1,000 requests per minute per API key.
blockers: New keys start with no permissions. Each module needs read or write granted, or calls fail with missing_endpoint_permission.
Errors come back as HTTP 200 with success set to false, so check the body, not the status code.
Confidential jobs, private fields and acting on behalf of a user each need their own toggle.
systems.request: An API key from an organization admin with only the modules the workflow needs, and the jobs and stages in scope.
systems.check: Every response has success set to true, and candidates land on the right job and stage.

risk.title: Failed Ashby calls look like successes
risk.detail: Ashby returns HTTP 200 with success set to false on errors, so a client that checks only status codes misses failed writes.
risk.mitigation: Check the success field on every response, and replay calls with a missing permission on purpose.

systems.name: Dayforce
systems.access: Dayforce REST web services. The customer creates a dedicated web services user whose role has the Web Services feature with Read Data, plus Post or Patch to write. Recruiting endpoints cover job postings, candidate sourcing and assessments.
systems.sandbox: The customer’s Dayforce test environment. Confirm whether Dayforce gives partners a developer sandbox; none is documented.
systems.limits: Set per client and per operation, and shared by every app. Dayforce’s one published example is 10 per second or 100 per minute for employee HR details.
blockers: Tokens come from the web services user’s username and password, last an hour and can’t be revoked. Plan how to cut access quickly if a credential leaks.
Call the client metadata endpoint at least daily to find the right service URL.
Field-level access for web services is set separately from the role.
Sourcing candidates from outside job boards depends on a Recruiting client setting. Confirm it is on.
systems.request: A dedicated web services user with a least-privilege role and field access, the test environment, and the requisitions in scope.
systems.check: Candidates and applications land on the right requisition in the test environment, and no extra fields are readable.

risk.title: A password login into the payroll system
risk.detail: Dayforce web services sign in as a user in the customer’s HCM and payroll system, and its tokens can’t be revoked, so security reviewers look hard at it.
risk.mitigation: Ask for a dedicated user with the narrowest role and field access, keep the password in the customer’s vault, and agree on a rotation drill.

systems.name: Smartsheet
systems.access: Smartsheet API 2.0 (REST). Server-to-server integrations use an API access token created in Smartsheet and sent as a Bearer token; Smartsheet recommends a shared service account. Integrations that act for each user use OAuth 2.0. Smartsheet Gov, EU and Australia have their own base URLs and tokens.
systems.sandbox: No free developer sandbox. Registering an OAuth app needs a licensed user on a Business plan or higher, so test in a separate workspace on a paid plan.
systems.limits: 300 requests per minute per token. Attachments and cell history count as 10 requests, capped at 30 per minute. OAuth access tokens last about 7 days and renew with the refresh token.
blockers: Pro and Free plans have no API access. Confirm the customer is on Business, Enterprise or Advanced Work Management.
Enterprise admins can set token expiry and revoke tokens, and a token tied to a person stops working when that person leaves. Ask for a service account.
Gov and EU customers are on separate instances; a token from smartsheet.com won’t work there.
systems.request: The plan and region, a service-account token or OAuth consent from a user who can edit the sheets in scope, the sheet IDs and column map, and any token-expiry policy.
systems.check: Rows land in the right sheet with the right column types, and a 429 is retried with backoff, not dropped.

risk.title: Smartsheet token tied to one person’s account
risk.detail: An API token has its owner’s sharing rights and stops working when that user is removed or an admin expiry policy applies.
risk.mitigation: Use a dedicated service account with access to only the sheets in scope, and alert on 401 errors.

systems.name: Microsoft Planner (premium) / Project
systems.access: Project for the web was retired into Planner in August 2025 and Project Online retired on September 30, 2026. Premium plans live in Dataverse (msdyn_project and related tables) and are written through the Project schedule APIs in an OperationSet. Basic plans use the Microsoft Graph Planner APIs. Every route needs an Entra ID app registration with tenant admin consent.
systems.sandbox: A non-production Dataverse environment in the customer’s tenant, or a developer or trial tenant with Planner and Project licenses.
systems.limits: Dataverse service protection limits per user: 6,000 requests and 20 minutes of execution time per 5 minutes, and 52 concurrent requests. Schedule APIs: up to 200 operations per OperationSet and 10 open OperationSets per user.
blockers: The Project schedule APIs accept only Project-licensed users, not application or integration users, so a background agent needs a licensed named account. That often fails security review.
Customers still on Project Online lost access on September 30, 2026. Find out where their plans went before building anything.
Confirm with Microsoft whether premium plans can be written through Graph; forum threads say premium tasks can be read but not written that way.
Tenant consent and Dataverse security roles often sit with separate Microsoft 365 and Power Platform admins.
systems.request: Where the plans live now (Planner basic, Planner premium or Project Server), the Dataverse environment URL, a licensed user for the schedule APIs, admin consent for the app, and the plans in scope.
systems.check: Tasks land in the right plan, bucket and assignee with the right dates, and a batch either commits fully or leaves nothing behind.

risk.title: Planner premium writes need a licensed user account
risk.detail: Microsoft blocks application users from the Project schedule APIs, so writes to premium plans need a Project-licensed user identity.
risk.mitigation: Agree on a dedicated licensed integration user in week 1. Otherwise limit the agent to basic plans or read-only queries.

systems.name: Esri ArcGIS (Online / Enterprise / Survey123)
systems.access: ArcGIS REST API. Writes go to a hosted feature layer, such as the one behind a Survey123 form, through applyEdits or addFeatures. Auth is an API key, OAuth 2.0 app credentials or a signed-in user. Creating credentials needs a Creator user type with the right privileges; API keys need ArcGIS Enterprise 11.4 or later.
systems.sandbox: ArcGIS Location Platform has a free monthly tier, but its layers can’t be shared publicly and it doesn’t support Survey123 webhooks. Test against a copy of the survey’s layer in the customer’s org.
systems.limits: No per-request applyEdits limit is published; confirm with Esri. Queries are capped per layer by maxRecordCount. ArcGIS Online feature storage uses credits (2.4 credits per 10 MB per month).
blockers: API keys and app credentials reach only items their creator owns, up to 100 items. If the survey layer belongs to someone else, ownership has to be sorted out first.
Esri advises against API keys for private layers with sensitive data, so county GIS teams may insist on OAuth app credentials or a named service user.
ArcGIS Enterprise portals are often behind the firewall or older than 11.4, which means IT tickets and no API keys.
Survey123 webhooks need change tracking turned on and can deliver the same event more than once.
systems.request: ArcGIS Online or Enterprise (and its version), the survey and its feature layer ID, a Creator account or admin to create the credential, and the field schema and domains per request type.
systems.check: Each replayed request lands as one feature with the right geometry, category and attributes, and a repeated webhook creates no duplicate.

risk.title: ArcGIS credentials can’t reach the survey layer
risk.detail: ArcGIS developer credentials only reach items their creator owns, and survey layers often belong to a GIS staffer or a Survey123 publisher account.
risk.mitigation: Have the layer owner or an admin create the credential in week 1, then test applyEdits against a copy of the layer.

systems.name: Shopify
systems.access: Shopify Admin API (GraphQL) through an app built in Shopify’s Dev Dashboard. Custom distribution installs on one store, or one Plus organization, without Shopify approval. Public distribution installs on many stores and needs Shopify’s review.
systems.sandbox: Development stores. Apps installed only on development stores need no data review.
systems.limits: Query cost limits by plan: 100 points per second on Standard, 200 on Advanced, 1,000 on Plus and 2,000 on Commerce Components. One query can’t cost more than 1,000 points.
blockers: Since January 1, 2026, merchants can’t create new custom apps in the Shopify admin. Build in the Dev Dashboard; existing admin-created apps keep working.
Public apps must request protected customer data access. Without approval, name, email, phone and address come back empty.
Confirm the review timeline. Shopify publishes none, and developers report waits of about 30 days in 2026.
The distribution method can’t be changed after you choose it.
systems.request: Install approval from the store owner, the scopes the workflow needs, and approval for each protected customer field if the app is public.
systems.check: Orders and customers match the store’s records, with no empty customer fields.

risk.title: Customer names, emails and phones come back empty
risk.detail: A public Shopify app gets protected customer fields only after Shopify approves each one. Until then the agent can’t see who it is calling or emailing.
risk.mitigation: Request each protected field on day 1, or use custom distribution for a single store while the review runs.

systems.name: Gorgias
systems.access: Gorgias REST API. A private integration uses an API key the customer’s admin creates, with HTTP Basic auth (account email and key). A public app uses OAuth 2.0, with access tokens that expire after 24 hours.
systems.sandbox: A trial account that Gorgias converts to a sandbox through its developer portal.
systems.limits: Leaky bucket: 80 requests per 20 seconds for OAuth apps and 40 for API keys, over 10 seconds on Enterprise. Calls past the limit return 429 with Retry-After.
blockers: A public OAuth app reaches customers only after Gorgias reviews it for the App Store.
An API key works with a user’s email, so use a dedicated integration user and its key.
If Gorgias’s own AI Agent or rules already answer tickets, decide which agent owns which tickets.
systems.request: An API key for a dedicated integration user (or OAuth install of your approved app), and the views, tags and rules in scope.
systems.check: Tickets get the right tags and assignee, and only one agent replies to each.

risk.title: Gorgias rules and the agent act on the same tickets
risk.detail: Rules and Gorgias’s AI Agent can tag, reply to or close a ticket the agent is working on.
risk.mitigation: List the rules that fire on the agent’s tickets, and split views or tags so each ticket has one owner.

systems.name: Klaviyo
systems.access: Klaviyo APIs with a private API key (full, read-only or custom scopes) or an OAuth app. Only Owner, Admin or Manager roles can create either.
systems.sandbox: A test account converted from a regular account; it can’t be converted back without support, and usage is still billed.
systems.limits: Burst and steady limits by endpoint tier, from 1 per second and 15 per minute (XS) to 350 per second and 3,500 per minute (XL). Private keys share one quota per account; OAuth apps get their own.
blockers: Private key scopes can’t be edited. To change them, delete the key and create a new one.
SMS needs explicit consent and a sending number. Implied consent doesn’t count, and double opt-in is the default.
A Marketplace listing needs OAuth, at least 5 active customer installs and Klaviyo’s review; an unlisted app installs by URL.
systems.request: A custom-scope private key (or OAuth install) from an Owner, Admin or Manager, and the lists, segments and flows in scope.
systems.check: Profiles and events land with the right consent status, and opt-outs sync back.

risk.title: Consent and opt-outs drift from Klaviyo
risk.detail: Klaviyo holds email and SMS consent. If the agent contacts people from another list, it can reach someone who unsubscribed in Klaviyo.
risk.mitigation: Read consent from Klaviyo before every outbound contact, and write opt-outs back right away.

systems.name: Applied Epic
systems.access: Applied Epic REST APIs through the Applied Dev Center. You build with test credentials, then request production access with the agency’s enterprise ID and Epic database name. The Epic SDK is the older route.
systems.sandbox: Test credentials from the Applied Dev Center. No copy of the agency’s database.
systems.limits: Not published. Confirm with Applied.
blockers: Applied approves each production app request before it issues credentials.
Applied says the agency needs an SDK-API license and a utility license. Confirm the cost and who pays.
Applied launched a Vendor Certification Program in August 2026. Confirm with Applied whether certification removes the agency’s license purchase; certified vendors say it does.
systems.request: Your production app request with the agency’s enterprise ID and database name, the agency’s API license status, and the policy and client objects in scope.
systems.check: Activities and policy updates land on the right client, policy and line of business.

risk.title: Applied approves production access per agency
risk.detail: Production credentials for each agency come only after Applied approves your request, and the agency may need to buy an API license first.
risk.mitigation: Submit the production request and confirm the agency’s license on day 1. Launch read-only, or with staff confirming in Epic, until it’s approved.

systems.name: Vertafore AMS360
systems.access: AMS360 Web Service API (SOAP). The agency admin creates a web service login and picks a data-security mode. Vertafore lists the API at no extra charge; its Orange Partner Program is a separate path.
systems.sandbox: None documented for agencies. Confirm with Vertafore; reports say Orange partners get a test instance.
systems.limits: Not published. Five failed logins lock the API login for 20 minutes.
blockers: Secured customers stay hidden from the API user until the agency calls Vertafore to turn on access for that API.
Confirm with Vertafore whether you must buy the Web Service SDK. Its help page says vendors writing programs need it.
A bad credential rollout trips the lockout and stops every call for 20 minutes.
systems.request: A dedicated web service login with the narrowest data-security mode, Vertafore access to secured customers if needed, and the customer and policy records in scope.
systems.check: Lookups return the same clients and policies staff see, including secured customers.

risk.title: Secured customers are invisible to the API
risk.detail: AMS360 hides secured customers from an API user until the agency asks Vertafore to open access, so lookups for those clients come back empty.
risk.mitigation: Ask the agency which customers are secured and request access from Vertafore on day 1. Replay lookups for secured clients.

systems.name: TazWorks (Instascreen)
systems.access: TazAPI: an XML gateway (Basic) or a JSON API with JWT tokens from an API application in the TazAPI developer portal (Advanced). A verification vendor that receives orders is set up as a data provider. Confirm the steps with TazWorks; integrators’ guides say TazWorks support enables the vendor, then each CRA admin enters your credentials and routes orders to you. TazWorks is part of MeridianLink.
systems.sandbox: The TazAPI developer portal gives a sample sandbox application, with separate test and production applications. Confirm a test setup for the data-provider route with TazWorks.
systems.limits: Not published. Confirm with TazWorks.
blockers: Confirm vendor enablement with TazWorks early; integrators’ guides say no CRA can route orders to you until TazWorks turns you on.
The data-provider spec, partner terms and fees aren’t public; the partner page is an application form.
Each CRA must add you as a vendor and set routing per search type. A missing routing rule means orders never reach the agent.
systems.request: Vendor enablement and the interface spec from TazWorks, the CRA’s TazWorks instance, an admin to route verification orders to you, and the order statuses the CRA expects back.
systems.check: Routed verification orders reach the agent, and each result returns to the same order and moves it to the CRA’s review status.

risk.title: TazWorks must turn your vendor on
risk.detail: Orders reach a verification vendor only after TazWorks enables it and each CRA sets routing, so neither you nor the CRA controls the start date.
risk.mitigation: Ask TazWorks for enablement and the interface spec in week 1, and confirm the steps. Until routing is live, CRA staff pass orders to you and key results back in.

systems.name: Accio Data
systems.access: Vendors write results into Accio’s XML interface, with documentation from Accio support. Since February 28, 2025 every integration must be registered with Accio, which issues an access key tied to the IP addresses you connect from. Each CRA client gives you its account credentials and endpoint.
systems.sandbox: Accio provides a sandbox after you’ve built the integration and sent your endpoint and product list. The vendor does its own testing.
systems.limits: Not published. Confirm with Accio Data.
blockers: The access key is tied to registered IP addresses, so an agent on cloud hosts with changing outbound IPs gets rejected.
Each licensee registers separately, so each new CRA customer can mean a new registration and key.
Accio says it doesn’t charge providers to integrate, but its FAQ says monthly minimums may apply. Confirm with Accio.
systems.request: Accio’s API documentation, your integration registration and access key, fixed outbound IPs, and the CRA’s Accio account and products in scope.
systems.check: Results posted with the key from a registered IP land on the right order, and posts from other IPs are rejected.

risk.title: Accio’s integration key is tied to your IP addresses
risk.detail: Accio accepts XML only with a registered access key sent from registered IP addresses, and each licensee registers separately.
risk.mitigation: Register in week 1 with fixed outbound IPs, and update the registration before changing hosting.

systems.name: ClearStar
systems.access: ClearStar is a CRA that runs its own screening platform. It publishes no API reference or vendor program; API documentation and custom integrations are available on request. Expect a direct agreement with ClearStar.
systems.sandbox: Not published. Confirm with ClearStar.
systems.limits: Not published. Confirm with ClearStar.
blockers: There is no public vendor program; access goes through ClearStar’s partnership and implementation teams.
ClearStar acts as the CRA itself, so its compliance team decides whether a verification vendor can work inside its orders.
Older filings describe a web services and HR-XML interface. Confirm with ClearStar which interface is current before you build.
systems.request: ClearStar’s API documentation and a test account, a named implementation contact, the verification types in scope, and the fields where results and contact attempts are written.
systems.check: Completed verifications appear on the right ClearStar order with source, contact and date, and no duplicate order is created.

risk.title: ClearStar has no public vendor program
risk.detail: ClearStar shares API documentation only on request and publishes no vendor terms, sandbox or limits, so scope and timing depend on ClearStar.
risk.mitigation: Get a named ClearStar contact and the documentation before committing to a date. Until then, staff enter the agent’s results in ClearStar.

systems.name: ezyVet (IDEXX)
systems.access: ezyVet REST API with OAuth 2.0 client credentials and a partner ID that IDEXX issues once it accepts you as a commercial partner. The practice then enables your partner integration in its ezyVet admin, selects the scopes and gives you the downloaded credentials files. Tokens last 12 hours.
systems.sandbox: Accepted commercial partners get a dedicated sandbox with API and UI logins. There is no self-serve sandbox before you apply.
systems.limits: Most endpoints allow 60 calls per minute, plus a global default of 180 calls per minute per database per partner. Over the limit returns 429, and ezyVet may disable a connection whose excess calls slow the site.
blockers: IDEXX accepts commercial partners that fit its product strategy, then requires an agreement and a certification demo.
Before general release you run a 6-week pilot with 5 clinics that consent in writing, and IDEXX issues the pilot credentials itself.
A clinic can’t hand an outside vendor its own private-integration credentials; ezyVet’s rules send vendors to the partner program.
systems.request: Your ezyVet partner status, the practice’s site and region, the credentials files with the scopes enabled, and the divisions (locations) in scope.
systems.check: Records sync to the right animal, consult and division, with no 429 errors at peak clinic hours.

risk.title: IDEXX partner certification and pilot come first
risk.detail: Without IDEXX commercial partner status there is no partner ID, and the path runs through an agreement, certification and a 5-clinic, 6-week pilot.
risk.mitigation: Apply in week 1, line up pilot clinics early, and throttle on the rate-limit headers.

systems.name: IDEXX Cornerstone
systems.access: Cornerstone runs on a server at each practice and has no public developer API. IDEXX takes requests through its practice management integration request form and lists approved Cornerstone integrations. Confirm with IDEXX which interface an approved partner gets, and before reading the Cornerstone database directly; IDEXX publishes no terms allowing it.
systems.sandbox: Not published. Confirm with IDEXX whether approved partners get a test Cornerstone install.
systems.limits: Not published. Confirm with IDEXX.
blockers: IDEXX reviews integration requests and publishes no criteria, fees or timeline. Confirm terms before promising a date.
An on-premises sync agent needs admin access to the Cornerstone server and outbound internet through the practice firewall, so practice IT must approve it.
Each hospital runs its own server and Cornerstone version. Confirm supported versions with IDEXX for every site in a multi-hospital group.
systems.request: Your IDEXX integration approval or submitted request, the Cornerstone version at each site, server admin access and an IT contact, and firewall rules for outbound traffic.
systems.check: Notes land on the right patient, client and visit, and the sync resumes after a server reboot.

risk.title: No public Cornerstone API, and IDEXX approval comes first
risk.detail: Cornerstone has no public third-party API, so access depends on IDEXX’s partner review plus software on each practice server.
risk.mitigation: Submit IDEXX’s integration request in week 1 and get the allowed access in writing. Until then, launch read-only or with staff pasting and confirming notes.

systems.name: Covetrus AVImark
systems.access: AVImark runs at the practice. Covetrus’s supported route is the Covetrus Connect API through its Technology Integration Partner Program, which it calls the only authenticated and supported way to integrate with its practice software. Confirm with Covetrus before reading AVImark data any other way.
systems.sandbox: Not published. Confirm with Covetrus.
systems.limits: Not published. Confirm with Covetrus.
blockers: Covetrus’s partner page says new integration requests are paused while it updates its APIs and partner framework (checked November 2026).
When requests reopen, expect an application and a partner agreement before you see API docs. Confirm the wait with Covetrus.
Each practice runs its own AVImark version. Confirm what Covetrus Connect supports for it.
systems.request: Your Covetrus Connect partner status or the date requests reopen, the AVImark version at each site, and the staff IDs and record sections in scope.
systems.check: Notes land in the right AVImark record sections, under the right patient and doctor.

risk.title: Covetrus has paused new integration requests
risk.detail: No supported route is open to a new vendor until Covetrus reopens its partner program, and Covetrus Connect is its only supported path.
risk.mitigation: Ask Covetrus for the reopening date now. Meanwhile, launch with staff confirming the agent’s output in AVImark, not an unsupported database connection.

systems.name: ModMed EMA (Modernizing Medicine)
systems.access: EMA Proprietary API (FHIR R4 style, read, search, create and update), reached through ModMed’s synapSYS program. ModMed provisions a sandbox, agrees the resources (ACLs) your app needs, runs a demo and technical review, then issues a production key. Each practice then generates its own credentials for your app. The Certified FHIR API is self-service but read and search only, so it can’t book.
systems.sandbox: ModMed provisions a generic sandbox after you join the synapSYS program and emails the credentials. Practice sandboxes also exist. The sandbox opens all resources; production gets only the resources ModMed approves.
systems.limits: 1,250 calls per minute per API key by default (about 20 per second). Over the limit returns 429. ModMed asks you to stagger calls and to contact your credential provisioner or synapsys@modmed.com for more.
blockers: No production key until ModMed’s demo, proof of concept and technical review pass, and resource provisioning can take up to two weeks after you request it.
Appointments and slots live in ModMed Practice Management. A practice on EMA alone has no scheduling data in the API, so booking needs ModMed PM.
Each practice must generate credentials for your app; ModMed publishes no fee for the Proprietary API. Confirm fees with ModMed.
The legacy password grant is being sunset, so build on the OAuth2 client credentials flow from the start.
systems.request: Your synapSYS sandbox and an MMI contact, the practice’s firm URL prefix, whether it runs ModMed PM or EMA alone, credentials the practice generates for your app, and the locations, providers and appointment types in scope.
systems.check: An appointment booked from a free slot lands in ModMed PM on the existing patient with the right provider, location and appointment type, and no duplicate patient is created.

risk.title: ModMed’s technical review gates production
risk.detail: ModMed issues a production key only after a demo, a sandbox proof of concept and a technical review of the resources you call and how often. Approved resources can take up to two weeks to provision.
risk.mitigation: Join synapSYS in week 1, list every resource (Appointment, Slot, Patient) in the first request, and book the review early. Until the key arrives, hand bookings to staff.

systems.name: Nextech
systems.access: Nextech Partner API (FHIR STU3, with R4 on Select) behind a registration process. A Nextech representative issues the credentials, and every call carries the practice ID. The practice orders your API in Nextech’s Community Portal, and Nextech reviews the order. Booking runs on the practice management side: Select (Book Appointment) or Practice+ (Create Appointment). The IntelleChartPRO API only reads patients and encounters.
systems.sandbox: Not published. Confirm with Nextech what test practice you get before production.
systems.limits: 20 requests per second per endpoint, enforced per user. Over the limit returns 429, and the limit can change. Nextech says the API is for real-time requests and asks partners to avoid bulk syncing in business hours.
blockers: Only a “Super Nextech Community User” at the practice can order your API, and the order then goes to Nextech for review. Confirm the turnaround with Nextech; one integrator’s guide says about 2 business days.

Select and Practice+ have different endpoints and auth (Select credentials must be reset through Microsoft on first login; Practice+ uses a partner ID and secret), so confirm which one the practice runs.
Fees for partner API access aren’t published, and Nextech says it doesn’t maintain third-party apps. Confirm fees and support terms with Nextech.
Nextech announced built-in AI patient-access partners (Assort Health, EliseAI) in October 2026, per press coverage. Confirm it doesn’t limit API scope for other voice vendors.
systems.request: Your Nextech developer registration, the practice’s Nextech practice ID, whether it runs Select or Practice+, the Community Portal order for your API, and the appointment types, purposes, providers and locations in scope.
systems.check: An appointment booked from a valid slot shows on the Nextech schedule as booked (not held) on the existing patient, with the right type, purpose, provider and location.

risk.title: Nextech issues credentials and the practice must order
risk.detail: Nextech hands out partner credentials only after registration, and each practice must order your API through its Community Portal for Nextech to review. Without both, the agent has no access.
risk.mitigation: Submit Nextech’s connection request form in week 1 and walk the practice’s Super Community User through the order on the first call. Until credentials arrive, hand bookings to staff.

systems.name: NextGen Enterprise / Office
systems.access: NextGen Enterprise: fill in the API Onboarding form, register in the NextGen Developer Portal, and join the API Distributor Program, which needs a signed agreement. The Global Service Account lets an app call most Enterprise API routes without a user launching it. NextGen Office: the certified APIs are read only (GET on USCDI v1 data), so there is no published booking path.
systems.sandbox: Enterprise developers get free, optional sandboxes for FHIR R4 and the Enterprise APIs, with test data. NextGen refreshes them monthly or quarterly and shares them with other developers. You must finish initial development there before beta. Not published for Office. Confirm with NextGen.
systems.limits: Enterprise: not published. Confirm with NextGen. Office: 20 requests per minute per IP address, 1,480 requests per 12 hours per Smart App Launch app, and one bulk request per patient per week.
blockers: NextGen’s standard API terms cover only USCDI GET routes. Any other route, including booking writes, needs NextGen’s prior written consent and Distributor terms, and using one in production without approval can end access.
Distributor fees vary with data scope and with read-only versus read and write, and NextGen doesn’t publish the amounts. Payment isn’t due until General Release. Confirm the fee with NextGen.
Beta must run with a participating NextGen client after a signed agreement and sandbox work, and NextGen publishes no review timeline.
On Office, the Smart App Launch or Bulk FHIR API costs $2,400 to onboard per vendor per practice, plus $50 or $100 a month, and still allows no writes.
systems.request: Whether the customer runs NextGen Enterprise (version 5.9 or later) or Office, your Developer Portal app and signed Distributor agreement, NextGen’s written approval for the appointment routes you need, the customer as beta site, and the locations, resources and event types in scope.
systems.check: An appointment booked through the approved route lands in the Enterprise PM appointment book on the existing patient with the right resource, location and event type, and no duplicate patient is created.

risk.title: Booking writes need NextGen’s written consent
risk.detail: NextGen’s standard API terms approve only read-only USCDI routes. Writing appointments needs separate Distributor terms, NextGen’s written consent, variable fees and a client beta, and Office has no write API at all.
risk.mitigation: File the Onboarding form in week 1, name the appointment routes in the Distributor request, and line up the customer as beta site. Until approval, read schedules only and hand bookings to staff.

systems.name: PioneerRx
systems.access: No self-serve developer signup. An outside vendor applies through PioneerRx’s Vendor Integration Inquiry form to become a Connected Vendor, and PioneerRx (RedSail Technologies) decides what it turns on. Its API docs describe endpoints the vendor hosts and PioneerRx calls (Patient Data Exchange, MTM Actions), a real-time prescription event feed PioneerRx can enable, and an Enterprise API, using basic auth plus ApplicationKey and LocationKey headers.
systems.sandbox: No sandbox or test pharmacy is published. Confirm with PioneerRx what test setup Connected Vendors get, and plan a pilot in one store.
systems.limits: Not published. Confirm with PioneerRx.
blockers: PioneerRx publishes no criteria, timeline or fee for becoming a Connected Vendor, and its API docs say they aren’t meant to be given to pharmacies, so the pharmacy can’t grant you access on its own.
Several integrations have PioneerRx call endpoints you host, so you need a public HTTPS endpoint that accepts PioneerRx’s auth headers before any data flows.
Setup is per store. Confirm the steps with PioneerRx; one integrator’s guide has staff enter the vendor’s endpoints in each location’s integration settings and restart PioneerRx before it goes live.
PioneerRx already lists AI phone and refill vendors such as Synerio and Pharmesol as Connected Vendors, so ask whether the pharmacy already pays for an overlapping tool.
systems.request: Your Connected Vendor status or inquiry, the NCPDP and NPI for each store, which PioneerRx integration will be enabled, one pilot store, and a BAA with the pharmacy.
systems.check: A refill taken by the agent lands on the right patient, Rx number and refill number, and shows in the right PioneerRx queue for staff review.

risk.title: PioneerRx must approve you as a Connected Vendor
risk.detail: There is no self-serve API. Access runs through PioneerRx’s vendor inquiry and its own setup, and PioneerRx publishes no timeline, fee or approval criteria.
risk.mitigation: Submit the Vendor Integration Inquiry in week 1 and have the pharmacy owner back the request. Until access exists, the agent takes refill requests and hands them to staff to enter in PioneerRx.

systems.name: Other pharmacy management system
systems.access: Most pharmacy systems publish no open API, and the vendor decides which outside products connect. McKesson EnterpriseRx is fully hosted by McKesson and certifies outside vendors on its interfaces through the pharmacy’s account executive. RedSail (PioneerRx, QS/1, BestRx) and Outcomes (Rx30) run their own vendor integrations. Confirm the path with the vendor named in the pharmacy’s contract.
systems.sandbox: None published by these vendors. Confirm what test environment the vendor provides, and plan a pilot in one store.
systems.limits: Not published. Confirm with the pharmacy system vendor.
blockers: Vendors approve integrations case by case and publish no fees or timelines. McKesson sends interface questions to the pharmacy’s account executive.

Renewal requests to prescribers (RxRenewal), change requests and CancelRx travel over Surescripts from the pharmacy system, which must be Surescripts-certified. Your agent can’t send them itself, so it has to hand the request to the pharmacy system.
Surescripts features are switched on per pharmacy. RedSail’s CancelRx guide says Surescripts Database Services must enable CancelRx for each participating pharmacy.
Systems are changing under you: CMS requires NCPDP SCRIPT v2023011 by January 1, 2028, and RedSail is retiring QS/1 NRx and migrating those pharmacies in waves.
systems.request: The pharmacy system name and version, the vendor’s written approval for your integration, the stores in scope, how refills and renewals reach the system today, and a BAA with the pharmacy.
systems.check: Refill requests from the agent appear in the pharmacy system on the right patient and prescription, and renewals to prescribers go out from the pharmacy system, not from the agent.

risk.title: The pharmacy system vendor controls access
risk.detail: There is usually no public API, and the vendor approves each outside integration on its own terms and schedule. The pharmacy can’t grant access by itself.
risk.mitigation: Name the system on the first call, contact its partner team in week 1, and get the pharmacy to sponsor the request. Until approval, the agent collects refill requests and staff enter them.

systems.name: PointClickCare
systems.access: Both PointClickCare programs start with its Apply for Partnership form, and PointClickCare decides which one fits. The USCDI Connector is a FHIR R4 API for USCDI v1 data with SMART on FHIR scopes, for patient, provider or bulk apps. The Marketplace program gives approved partners PointClickCare’s APIs for an authorized use case. PointClickCare approves your Developer Portal account, and each customer enables you by facility.
systems.sandbox: USCDI Connector development apps are auto-approved in a shared PointClickCare FHIR sandbox with test logins. Production apps need PointClickCare’s approval. Confirm what sandbox the Marketplace program gives you.
systems.limits: No rate limits are published. PointClickCare’s API terms say it may cap the data some queries return, require paging, and throttle or suspend an app that threatens stability or security. Confirm with PointClickCare.
blockers: Each app needs PointClickCare’s written approval and a Letter of Authorization from each customer, then enablement by facility that takes at least 2 weeks.

USCDI Connector customers pay a flat $65 per app per facility per month (checked November 2026). Confirm current Marketplace terms; a 2020 partner agreement filed in a public securities filing charges partners a per-facility monthly fee with a minimum facility commitment.
You must sign a BAA, or the Canadian equivalent, with each customer, and the Marketplace agreement bars access from outside Canada or the U.S.
Marketplace apps pass PointClickCare’s App Validation, and PointClickCare can require it again after material changes to the app.
systems.request: Your PointClickCare program and partner status, the customer’s Letter of Authorization, the facilities and tenant ID, the scopes you need, and a BAA or PHIPA agent agreement with the operator.
systems.check: Data pulled for one facility matches the residents and active orders staff see in PointClickCare, with no residents from other facilities and complete paging on large pulls.

risk.title: Approval and per-facility fees gate each home
risk.detail: PointClickCare must approve the app, each customer must authorize it in writing and enable it by facility, and fees run per facility per month.
risk.mitigation: Apply for partnership in week 1, get the operator’s Letter of Authorization signed early, price the per-facility fee into the deal, and start with one facility. Until enablement, staff export the reports the agent needs.

systems.name: CDK Global (Fortellis / 3PA)
systems.access: CDK DMS APIs through Fortellis, CDK’s developer network. CDK has moved app vendors from its older CDK Global Partner Program to Fortellis. You register an app in a verified Fortellis organization, pick CDK APIs and their pricing plans, accept CDK’s API terms and pay to start certification. After certification and a reviewed Marketplace listing, each dealer activates your app, and every call carries that dealer’s Subscription ID plus an OAuth token from your app credentials.
systems.sandbox: Fortellis has a Test environment that mirrors Production, and you validate your app there before certification. The API Directory’s call tester only shows request mechanics with example data from the spec. Confirm with CDK what test dealer data you get.
systems.limits: Each API’s pricing plan can rate limit you, and usage above the plan is charged as an overage or denied. Per-API numbers aren’t published publicly. Confirm them on the plans shown at registration.
blockers: Fortellis charges a one-time Onboarding Service Fee of $4,500 USD ($6,075 CAD) to start certification and $169 USD ($229 CAD) per month once your app is listed, plus each CDK API’s own plan (checked November 2026). CDK can change its API fees by posting them.

CDK’s API terms limit use to the apps named in your order, require CDK’s written approval for any other use, require a signed enrollment from each dealer, and bar any access to CDK systems not authorized by CDK. CDK has blocked integrators that used dealer logins since August 2015.
Either side can end the API terms on 30 days’ notice, and CDK can block access for late payment or end it at once for a breach.

Data access has been costly and contested. In 2017 court testimony, 3PA cost one vendor $735 per dealer per month, up from about $160 in 2014, and in 2025 CDK agreed to pay $630 million to settle a vendor class’s price claims. Confirm current per-API prices before quoting the dealer.
systems.request: Your Fortellis organization and app ID, the CDK APIs and plans you selected, each rooftop’s signed enrollment and Subscription ID, the stores in scope, and a named dealer contact who can activate the app.
systems.check: Every call uses the right rooftop’s Subscription ID, and writes land on the existing customer and vehicle in CDK with no duplicate customer records.

risk.title: CDK allows access only through Fortellis, after certification
risk.detail: CDK’s API terms bar access to CDK systems by any means it hasn’t authorized, and CDK has blocked integrators using dealer logins since 2015. Until your Fortellis app is certified and each dealer enrolls, the agent has no approved way in.
risk.mitigation: Register the app and pay the onboarding fee in week 1, and get each rooftop’s enrollment early. Until certification, have staff enter the agent’s output into CDK. Plan a manual fallback too: a June 2024 cyberattack took CDK dealers’ DMS offline for days.

systems.name: Reynolds and Reynolds (RCI)
systems.access: Reynolds Certified Interface (RCI) only. A vendor submits the RCI Participant Interest Form on reyrey.com (or writes to RCI@reyrey.com), then goes through certification for a specific application and a specific set of data components. Reynolds builds the interface for each certified participant and re-certifies it over time. RCI covers the ERA, POWER and Reynolds CRM systems.
systems.sandbox: Not published. Confirm with Reynolds what test environment certification uses.
systems.limits: Not published. Confirm with Reynolds. You only get the data components your application is certified for.
blockers: Reynolds has never accepted a dealer’s authorization alone. A federal court found in 2017 that Reynolds allows third-party access only with its own approval, its RCI contract treats any access without its written consent as Non-Approved Access, and its dealer agreements bar giving passwords to non-employees.
Reynolds detects and disconnects automated access. It began blocking a data integrator in 2009 and blocked it effectively by 2013.

RCI prices aren’t public, and the standard RCI contract barred vendors from discussing them. In 2017 court testimony, one vendor’s RCI package rose from $247 per dealer per month in 2011 to $893 in 2017, and another paid about $835 plus write-back fees. Confirm current pricing with Reynolds.
A pre-certified vendor can’t market or ship a certified interface until Reynolds certifies the specific application. No timeline is published.
systems.request: Whether each store runs ERA-IGNITE or POWER, the stores in scope, your RCI status for this application and its data components, write-back approval if the agent writes, and the dealer’s signed authorization.
systems.check: The agent reads only its certified data fields, and any write-back lands on the right customer, vehicle and repair order in ERA.

risk.title: Reynolds blocks any access outside RCI
risk.detail: Reynolds’ licenses forbid third-party access on dealer logins, and it detects and cuts off automated sessions. In 2017 the Seventh Circuit vacated an injunction that had forced Reynolds to allow that access, so a dealer can’t authorize you around RCI.
risk.mitigation: Submit the RCI interest form in week 1 and scope the smallest data set the workflow needs. Until certification, deliver the agent’s output to staff to enter, or work from reports the dealer runs itself.

systems.name: Tekion
systems.access: Tekion Automotive Partner Cloud (APC) APIs and webhooks. You register at apc.tekioncloud.com, accept Tekion’s API License and Data Sharing Agreement, describe your use case and pick APIs, and Tekion approves you before you get the API documentation and a token. The dealer then authorizes your integration in its Integration Hub.
systems.sandbox: Not published. Confirm with Tekion whether approved partners get a test dealer environment.
systems.limits: Standard partners get standard rate limits and Enterprise partners get higher ones, but the numbers aren’t published. Tekion can revoke access for an unusual number or frequency of requests. Confirm history depth too: a 2023 forum post said one API returned only the last 7 days.
blockers: Tekion reviews each application and publishes no criteria or timeline. Additional APIs and higher rate limits sit in the Enterprise tier.
The API agreement allows integration only through documented APIs, bars sharing your token, and limits data use to the uses listed in its Schedule 1.
Either party can end the API agreement at any time for any reason, which ends your license.
Confirm pricing for your tier with Tekion. In a 2023 dealer forum thread, a Tekion representative said most integrations are free and heavier use is charged through Enterprise and premium plans.
systems.request: Your APC approval and tier, the APIs and webhooks approved for your use case, the dealer’s authorization in Integration Hub, and the rooftops in scope.
systems.check: Records written through the API land on the right customer, vehicle and rooftop, and webhook events match what staff see in Tekion.

risk.title: Tekion approval and tier decide what the agent can reach
risk.detail: Without APC approval there is no token, and the tier Tekion grants sets which APIs and rate limits you get. Tekion can end the API agreement at any time.
risk.mitigation: Register in week 1 with a narrow use case, confirm the tier covers every API the workflow needs, and throttle well below the limits. Have staff handle any step whose API isn’t in your tier.

systems.name: McLeod (LoadMaster / PowerBroker)
systems.access: McLeod REST web services for LoadMaster (carriers) and PowerBroker (brokers), returning JSON or XML. Two routes: the cloud-hosted APIs in McLeod’s Innovation Hub, where you register, request a key per API and send X-Api-Key plus the customer’s X-Mcld-Tenant header; or the customer’s own server, where calls use Basic auth or a bearer token that the customer’s admin registers inside LoadMaster or PowerBroker. Calls enforce the same permissions and validations as the desktop app.
systems.sandbox: The Innovation Hub offers trial keys and a documentation sandbox for trying calls, and a central Direct-Hosted sandbox server that McLeod says is only for viewing and testing API results. There is no published test copy of a customer’s own data; ask the customer for a test or training company.
systems.limits: Not published. Confirm with McLeod.
blockers: McLeod issues Innovation Hub keys per API on request and certifies partners, but publishes no criteria, fee or timeline for either. Confirm them with McLeod early.
Confirm the customer licenses McLeod’s API module. McLeod’s API page describes the published services as an API module and offers custom APIs for customers.

Confirm whether the customer runs McLeod on its own servers or McLeod hosts it. Customer-hosted systems need network access to the customer’s server, and the cloud-hosted APIs need the tenant ID from McLeod.
Order Creation requests may be auto-accepted or held for review depending on the tenant’s settings, so a booked load may not exist until staff accept it.
systems.request: LoadMaster or PowerBroker and the version, who hosts it, whether the API module is licensed, a dedicated McLeod user or token for your agent with the narrowest role, the tenant ID if using cloud-hosted APIs, and a test company.
systems.check: Orders created by the agent land on the right customer with the right stops, appointment windows, equipment and rate, show the agent’s user in the audit trail, and no duplicate order is created on retry.

risk.title: McLeod keys and certification are not self-serve
risk.detail: Cloud-hosted API keys are requested per API and approved by McLeod, and McLeod’s supported route for outside vendors is its certified partner network. Neither the criteria, fees nor timeline are published.
risk.mitigation: Register on the Innovation Hub and request keys in week 1, and email McLeod partnerships about certification. Until approved, use a customer-issued token on the customer’s own server if the customer agrees, or hand staff a draft that they enter in McLeod.

systems.name: Oracle Transportation Management (OTM)
systems.access: OTM (now Oracle Fusion Cloud Transportation and Global Trade Management) REST API for business objects such as order releases, shipments and locations, plus a data export API. The customer’s admin creates an integration user and grants per-resource view or update rights. Auth is OAuth 2 client credentials through an Oracle Identity Cloud Service app whose client ID is set on that user, or Basic auth on the resources-int path, which the customer can disable.
systems.sandbox: Every subscription includes one Test instance and one Production instance; extra test instances depend on the customer’s contract. Oracle offers no public developer sandbox, so you test in the customer’s Test instance.
systems.limits: Paging defaults to 25 records and is capped at 1,000 per request, a limit Oracle says can’t be raised. The customer can set a lower cap, and Oracle Ops can cap data per collection. Oracle publishes no request rate limit. Confirm with Oracle and the customer.
blockers: The customer’s OTM admin must create the integration user and grant view and update rights on each REST resource you need. Missing rights block calls.
OAuth 2 needs a confidential app in the customer’s Oracle identity domain, set up by their identity admin, and the client ID added to the OTM integration user.

Test and Production update on different quarterly cadences, so an Oracle update can reach Test first and change behavior. Oracle tells customers to rerun integration tests before each production update.
systems.request: The OTM release, the Test and Production URLs, an integration user with only the REST resource rights you need, an OAuth client from their identity admin, the domain in scope, and a Test instance refreshed from Production.
systems.check: Order releases or shipments posted by the agent appear in the right domain with the right locations, dates and reference numbers, paging past 1,000 records returns every record, and the same replay passes again after the next quarterly update on Test.

risk.title: Two admins must set up access before any call works
risk.detail: OTM access needs an integration user with per-resource rights from the OTM admin and an OAuth client from the identity admin. Basic auth can be turned off, so there is no shortcut.
risk.mitigation: Send the exact resource list and the OAuth steps from Oracle’s Integration Guide in week 1 and test access on the Test instance first. Until access exists, deliver files that staff load through the customer’s existing OTM integration.

systems.name: Opendock (dock scheduling)
systems.access: Opendock (a Loadsmart product) Nova REST API. A carrier registers a free Opendock account, links it to its carrier company by USDOT number or name, then exchanges email and password for a JWT at POST /auth/login. With that token the agent searches warehouses, reads load types and open times, and creates appointments. Warehouses use the same API with their own users, and a socket.io stream pushes appointment changes.
systems.sandbox: Opendock runs a staging server, neutron.staging.opendock.com, for testing; Opendock says it is not for production and is subject to changes and resets. Confirm that staging has a test warehouse your carrier account can book.
systems.limits: Not published. JWT lifetime depends on the user’s role. The event stream does not replay events missed while disconnected. Confirm limits with Opendock.
blockers: Each warehouse sets its own rules: required reference (PO) numbers, custom fields, documents to upload and which load types carriers may book. A booking that misses one is rejected.
Some warehouses must confirm bookings, so a new appointment can sit in Requested status rather than Scheduled.

Auth is a user login, not an API key. Confirm with Loadsmart that an agent may book under a carrier user. opendock.com/terms points to Loadsmart’s subscription agreement, which limits access to the customer’s employees.
systems.request: A dedicated Opendock carrier user for your agent tied to the carrier’s company, the list of warehouses and their reference number formats, who at the carrier gets the confirmation emails, and Loadsmart’s written OK for automated booking.
systems.check: An appointment booked by the agent shows at the right warehouse, dock, load type and local start time with the right PO number, reaches Scheduled status or is flagged when it stays Requested, and the time is written back to the load in the carrier’s TMS.

risk.title: Opendock’s terms may not cover an agent using a carrier login
risk.detail: Opendock books through a named user’s email and password, and the terms opendock.com links to limit access to the customer’s own employees. Loadsmart says tens of thousands of appointments a month are booked by API, but no published term addresses an outside agent booking for a carrier.
risk.mitigation: Ask Loadsmart in week 1 to confirm in writing that your agent may book for carriers under a dedicated user. Until then, have the agent find open slots and draft the booking, and let carrier staff submit it.

systems.name: Guidewire (PolicyCenter / ClaimCenter)
systems.access: Guidewire Cloud API, a REST API on the carrier’s PolicyCenter or ClaimCenter. Every caller app must be registered with Guidewire Hub before it can get tokens: the carrier contacts Guidewire, Guidewire registers the app and sends back a client ID and secret. A server-side agent uses the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow as a standalone service, and the carrier’s API role decides which endpoints and fields it can reach.
systems.sandbox: Carriers on Guidewire Cloud have dev, QA and UAT planets in non-production star systems, plus preprod. Ask the carrier for access to one. Guidewire publishes no self-serve sandbox for outside vendors; Marketplace partners build and test validated integrations, but the environment terms aren’t published. Confirm with Guidewire.
systems.limits: Each resource has a maximum page size; the default is 25 per page and the maximum 100, and the carrier can change both per resource. Total counts stop at 1,000. Rate limits are not published. Confirm with Guidewire and the carrier.
blockers: You can’t register yourself. The carrier must ask Guidewire to register your app with Guidewire Hub, and you get nothing until Guidewire returns the client ID and secret.

API roles are allowlists and a new caller has no endpoint access, so the carrier must build a role for your service. Authority limits and permissions are checked against the carrier’s proxy service user.

Listing on the Guidewire Marketplace takes an application, a PartnerConnect agreement and a scope document approved by Guidewire’s engineering validation team within six months. Fees aren’t published. Confirm whether the carrier requires it.
The Cloud API docs cover Guidewire Cloud releases. Confirm whether the carrier runs Guidewire Cloud or a self-managed install, and which APIs a self-managed system exposes.
systems.request: Whether the carrier runs Guidewire Cloud (and which release) or self-managed, a Guidewire Hub registration for a standalone service with client ID and secret, an API role limited to the endpoints in scope, the proxy service user’s authority limits, a dev or UAT planet with test claims, and the lines of business in scope.
systems.check: Notes, documents or activities the agent writes land on the right claim and exposure under the carrier’s service user, and a call to an endpoint outside your API role is refused.

risk.title: The carrier must register you and grant an API role
risk.detail: Only Guidewire can register your app with Guidewire Hub, and only after the carrier asks. Even then you have no endpoint access until the carrier’s team builds an API role for you, so go-live rides on the carrier’s Guidewire backlog.
risk.mitigation: In week 1, send the carrier the exact auth flow (standalone service) and the endpoints and fields you need so it can file the Guidewire request and draft the role together. Until credentials arrive, deliver drafts that adjusters enter in ClaimCenter.

systems.name: Duck Creek (Policy / Claims)
systems.access: Duck Creek publishes no public API reference. It describes Duck Creek Anywhere as a REST API and its Integration Hub as insurance-ready APIs and prebuilt connections. Outside vendors go through the Duck Creek partner ecosystem: integrations are built for Duck Creek to validate and list on its Content Exchange, and the carrier, on OnDemand (Duck Creek’s SaaS) or its own install, controls the credentials. Confirm the auth method with Duck Creek.
systems.sandbox: Not published. Confirm with Duck Creek whether partners get a development environment, or use the carrier’s non-production environment.
systems.limits: Not published. Confirm with Duck Creek.
blockers: Partnership starts with a request form reviewed by Duck Creek’s Partner Ecosystem team. Requirements, fees and timeline aren’t published. Confirm them early.
API docs aren’t public, so you can’t scope the work until Duck Creek or the carrier gives you access.

Content Exchange packages can ship as source code and SQL scripts installed with Duck Creek’s Package Utility, some with manual steps. Confirm who installs and tests yours on the carrier’s environment.

Duck Creek launched an Agentic AI Platform on April 28, 2026, with an AI Gateway that uses MCP and A2A to connect partner agents. Confirm with the carrier whether outside agents must connect through it.
systems.request: Whether the carrier is on Duck Creek OnDemand or self-hosted, the Policy or Claims release, an introduction to its Duck Creek account team, a non-production environment, the API or integration method Duck Creek approves for your use, and the lines of business in scope.
systems.check: Claim notes, tasks or policy updates the agent writes appear on the right claim or policy in Duck Creek, and the same lookups return what adjusters see.

risk.title: Duck Creek’s API path isn’t public
risk.detail: Duck Creek publishes no API reference, sandbox, limits or partner terms, so cost and timeline stay unknown until its partner team and the carrier engage.
risk.mitigation: Submit the partner request form in week 1 with the carrier’s sponsorship, and ask the carrier’s Duck Creek team for the approved integration method. Until then, deliver outputs that staff enter in Duck Creek.

systems.name: Archer (Archer IRM)
systems.access: Archer offers a Web Services API (SOAP), a RESTful API and a Content API. For REST, you POST the instance name, user name, domain and password to /platformapi/core/security/login and send the returned token as an Archer session-id Authorization header. The bank’s Archer admin creates the user, and every call is limited by that user’s Archer permissions. There’s no published OAuth or API key option.
systems.sandbox: Archer publishes no vendor sandbox. Ask the bank for access to its non-production Archer instance, and confirm with the bank that its Archer license covers your use there.
systems.limits: Not published. Confirm with Archer and the bank.
blockers: With single sign-on on, the RESTful API only issues a session token if Allow manual bypass is selected in Archer Control Panel. The Web Services API can issue one without it. Either way the bank’s security team must approve a password-based service account.
The bank’s admin must build an access role that covers only the applications in scope, such as third-party profiles, assessments and findings.
Confirm the bank’s Archer release, SaaS or on-premises, and base path. The REST base URL moved from /api/ to /platformapi/ in release 6.5.
Confirm session handling with Archer. Community forum posts say a second login with the same account ends the first session, so parallel workers need separate accounts.
systems.request: The bank’s Archer release and deployment, the base URL, a dedicated Archer user with an access role limited to the applications in scope, the bank’s decision on SSO manual bypass or the Web Services login, a non-production instance, and the application and field IDs you will read or write.
systems.check: Records the agent creates or updates appear in the right Archer application with the right field values and record permissions, and a request outside the service user’s access role is refused.

risk.title: Bank security must approve a password login for the agent
risk.detail: Archer’s REST login takes a user name and password, and on SSO instances it needs Allow manual bypass. Many bank security teams won’t approve a password-based account that skips SSO without review.
risk.mitigation: Raise the login method in the week 1 security review and offer the Web Services login path, a narrow access role and IP restrictions. Until approved, deliver files that staff import or enter in Archer.

systems.name: Clio (Manage)
systems.access: Clio Manage API v4 (REST) with OAuth 2.0 authorization code. You register a developer application in Clio’s developer portal for each region your customers use: US, CA, EU and AU each have their own portal, API host and app ID. A Clio user at the firm authorizes your app, and the token works only in that region. Access tokens last 30 days; refresh tokens don’t expire.
systems.sandbox: Clio has no separate sandbox. You sign up for a 7-day Clio Manage trial in each region you need, then apply to have Clio convert it to a free developer account. Clio reviews the request, so conversion isn’t automatic.
systems.limits: 50 requests per minute per access token during peak hours (US/CA 04:00 to 19:00 Pacific, Monday to Friday; EU and AU have their own windows), higher off-peak. Over the limit returns 429 with Retry-After. Some endpoints have their own limits, and Clio doesn’t grant custom increases (checked November 2026).
blockers: The authorizing user’s role applies on top of your app permissions. If billing rate or hours visibility is restricted, time entries come back with prices or hours redacted, and updates to redacted fields return 403.
App permissions are fixed when a user authorizes. Adding one later, such as write access to activities, means every user has to authorize again.
Confirm the firm’s plan. Clio’s private-app guide says apps and integrations aren’t available on the EasyStart tier.

Clio’s docs don’t say whether an unlisted app may serve many firms. An App Directory listing needs Clio’s security and compliance questionnaire, a demo and a listing review, with no published timeline or fee. Confirm with Clio’s API partnerships team.
systems.request: The firm’s Clio region and plan, a user to authorize your app whose role can see and edit time entries and billing rates, the matters and timekeepers in scope, and who reviews entries before bills go out.
systems.check: Time entries land on the right matter and user with the right date, hours, rate and description, with no redacted fields and no 429 errors during peak hours.

risk.title: The authorizing user’s role limits what the agent sees
risk.detail: Clio applies the user’s role on top of app permissions. With restricted billing rate or hours visibility, time entry prices and hours come back null or redacted and writes to those fields fail with 403, so the agent drafts against incomplete data.
risk.mitigation: In week 1 have the firm admin pick an authorizing user whose role sees all billing data, register the app in the firm’s region, and test one read and one write on a real matter. Until that passes, staff enter time from the agent’s drafts.

systems.name: SurePoint (LMS)
systems.access: SurePoint publishes no developer portal or API docs. Its site now sells LMS as SurePoint Finance Enterprise (formerly LMS), hosted on AWS. Confirm the connection method with SurePoint; one integrator’s help guide says a SurePoint-issued service account is required and the firm requests it from its SurePoint account manager. A PointOne case study describes client and matter sync every 15 minutes and approved entries landing in LMS5 for pre-bill review.
systems.sandbox: Not published. Confirm with SurePoint whether a test environment exists for the firm’s LMS version.
systems.limits: Not published. Confirm with SurePoint.
blockers: The service account comes from SurePoint, not the firm’s own admin. Confirm the lead time and any fee with the firm’s SurePoint account manager; one integrator’s guide says the account needs rights to sign in, read data and create time entries.

SurePoint’s partner page invites software providers to apply by email and says an integration is either available, can be developed for a customer, or is planned. It publishes no criteria, agreement or fee. Confirm them with SurePoint.
Confirm how LMS matches timekeepers. One integrator’s FAQ says releases fail with “user not found” unless the attorney’s email in LMS matches exactly.
Confirm what LMS does with entries that break the firm’s narrative rules. One integrator’s FAQ says LMS can reject them without returning an error.
systems.request: The firm’s SurePoint product and version (LMS5, LMS+, LMS V or Finance Enterprise), a dedicated service account from SurePoint with read and create-time rights, API documentation for that version, the timekeepers with their emails as stored in LMS, and the firm’s narrative and billing-code rules.
systems.check: Every released entry appears in LMS pre-bill review on the right client, matter, timekeeper and billing code, and the count in LMS matches the count the agent sent.

risk.title: Access depends on SurePoint, with no public API docs
risk.detail: SurePoint publishes no API documentation, limits or partner terms, so the connection method, scope and lead time stay unknown until SurePoint answers. Confirm the details; one integrator’s guide says a SurePoint-issued service account is required and rejected entries may not return errors.
risk.mitigation: In week 1 have the firm ask its SurePoint account manager for a service account and API docs, and email SurePoint’s partnerships team. Until access works, deliver drafted entries for staff to key into LMS, and reconcile counts after every release.

systems.name: Elite 3E
systems.access: 3E REST and OData APIs covering clients, matters, time, timekeepers and costs. On 3E Cloud the firm enables access in its own Microsoft Entra ID with an app registration and gives you the OAuth 2.0 token URL, client ID, secret, scope and its 3E instance ID. Use delegated permissions (authorization code) when acting for a user so 3E ethical walls apply. On-premises 3E (2.8.1 and later) exposes the API on the firm’s server with Windows authentication.
systems.sandbox: Elite partners can request credentials for Elite’s Partner API Test Instance from partnerprogram@elite.com. Without partner status, test on the firm’s own non-production 3E instance; confirm the firm has one.
systems.limits: 3E Cloud: 30 calls per minute for REST and 60 per minute for OData, with OData pages capped at 5,000 rows; throttling starts when you go over. On-premises firms set their own limits. For bulk extraction Elite points to 3E Change Stream webhooks (checked November 2026).
blockers: The firm’s Entra ID admin must register the app, add the 3E API permissions and grant admin consent, and the firm must give you the instance ID for each environment.
On-premises 3E uses Windows authentication on the firm’s network, so firm IT must approve a domain account and network access for the agent.
30 REST calls per minute on 3E Cloud is low for syncing time across many timekeepers, so writes have to be queued and batched.
Premier Technology Partner status means Elite certification and ongoing compatibility testing. Elite publishes no criteria, timeline or fee. Confirm with Elite.
systems.request: Whether the firm runs 3E Cloud or on-premises and which version, an Entra ID app registration with delegated 3E API permissions and admin consent (token URL, client ID, secret, scope), the instance IDs for test and production, and the timekeepers and matters in scope.
systems.check: Time cards created through the API pass 3E validation and land as pending time on the right matter, timekeeper and task code, with walled matters invisible to the agent and no throttling at 30 calls per minute.

risk.title: 3E Cloud allows 30 REST calls a minute
risk.detail: Elite caps 3E Cloud REST at 30 calls per minute and OData at 60, and says the APIs are meant for lower-volume integrations. A sync that polls matters and posts one time card per call hits the cap when many timekeepers release time at once.
risk.mitigation: In week 1 measure calls per synced entry, queue writes with backoff, and take matter changes from 3E Change Stream instead of polling. If the queue backs up, staff post time from a reviewed export.

systems.name: Oracle OPERA Cloud (OHIP)
systems.access: OPERA Cloud REST and streaming APIs through the Oracle Hospitality Integration Platform (OHIP). A vendor registers an application in the OHIP partner developer portal and gets an application key. To reach a hotel’s production environment, the hotel creates an integration user in its OPERA Cloud tenancy, its chain administrator approves it, and you add that environment in your portal. Hotels must not share credentials from their own OHIP portal with vendors.
systems.sandbox: A partner sandbox shared by more than 1,300 companies, so other developers’ activity shows up in it. Calls in the sandbox are billed like production calls.
systems.limits: 50 requests per second per gateway, shared by every consumer of that gateway, with short bursts to 100; over the limit returns 429. Only one client per chain and application key can consume the event stream (checked November 2026).
blockers: Oracle grants access to production OPERA Cloud environments only after your solution is listed in the Oracle Hospitality Cloud Marketplace under OHIP, which needs an Oracle PartnerNetwork membership.
OHIP is a pay-as-you-go subscription with no free tier, and the owner of the application key pays for every call. Oracle’s FAQ puts calls above the 10,000-transaction plan at about USD 20 per 10,000.
The hotel’s chain administrator must approve your integration user before you can add the environment, so each new hotel group waits on its own admin.
systems.request: The hotel’s chain and property codes, an integration user approved by the chain administrator, the environment name and enterprise ID from the hotel’s OHIP portal, and the room types, rate codes and packages the agent may book.
systems.check: Reservations land in OPERA Cloud on the right property, room type and rate code, attached to an existing guest profile when one exists, with no duplicate profile.

risk.title: Production OPERA Cloud access needs an Oracle Marketplace listing
risk.detail: Oracle opens production OPERA Cloud environments to a vendor only after it lists its solution in the Oracle Hospitality Cloud Marketplace, and every API call, including sandbox calls, is billed to the vendor’s application key.
risk.mitigation: Join Oracle PartnerNetwork and submit the Marketplace listing in week 1, and budget OHIP calls from replay volume. Until production access arrives, the agent takes booking requests and staff enter them in OPERA.

systems.name: Mews
systems.access: Mews Connector API. Every request carries a ClientToken that identifies your application, which Mews’s integration team issues after certification, and an AccessToken for each property, which the property’s admin provides. Mews says the API is free to access and use.
systems.sandbox: A public demo environment with shared test tokens and no real data. Replay real bookings only against the hotel’s own account after certification.
systems.limits: 200 requests per AccessToken within 30 seconds, on a sliding window, in demo and production. Over the limit returns 429 with Retry-After. Mews calls the limits best-effort and says they may change without notice.
blockers: You register through the Mews Marketplace form, test in demo and submit a certification form. Mews checks your demo requests against the operations and purpose you list, and publishes no timeline.
Certification covers the operations you list, so a write you add later, such as cancelling reservations, needs to be in scope first.
Each property’s admin must give you its AccessToken.
systems.request: Your Mews certification status, an AccessToken from each property’s admin, and the services, resource categories (room types) and rates the agent may book.
systems.check: Reservations land in Mews on the right service, room category and rate, attached to the existing customer when one exists, with no 429 errors at peak.

risk.title: No production token until Mews certifies your requests
risk.detail: Mews issues the production ClientToken only after it reviews your demo-environment requests against the operations and purpose you declared, and it publishes no timeline.
risk.mitigation: Register and build against the demo environment in week 1, and list every operation the agent needs, including reservation writes, on the certification form. Until certified, the agent takes requests and staff book them in Mews.

systems.name: Cloudbeds
systems.access: Cloudbeds REST API. A technology partner’s app gets access when a Cloudbeds user at the property grants it through OAuth 2.0. Properties can also use the API for their own integrations, which Cloudbeds calls a self-service feature. Partners apply through Cloudbeds’ technology partner page.
systems.sandbox: Not published. Confirm with Cloudbeds whether partners get a test property.
systems.limits: Cloudbeds’ FAQ says 5 requests per second for properties and 10 for technology partners, and its tech specs list 10 per second for all endpoints. Going over can get API credentials suspended for a time.
blockers: Cloudbeds requires a minimum of 5 pilot properties, and up to 10 for the official go-live, before a partner integration is generally available.
The API license makes certification your expense, and significant changes to your app need re-certification.
The license bars using personal data from the API for anything beyond the allowed use, so check that model training or analytics on guest data is covered.
