systems.request: Your Cloudbeds partner status, a property user to grant OAuth access, the pilot properties lined up, and the room types and rate plans the agent may book.
systems.check: Reservations land in Cloudbeds on the right property, room type and rate plan, and the agent stays under the per-second limit at peak.

risk.title: Cloudbeds wants 5 to 10 pilot properties
risk.detail: Cloudbeds asks technology partners for at least 5 pilot properties and up to 10 for the official go-live, and certification is at your expense.
risk.mitigation: Line up pilot properties and apply in week 1. For a single hotel, ask whether it can use the API under its own self-service access while partner status is pending.

systems.name: Stayntouch PMS
systems.access: Stayntouch Connect API with OAuth 2.0 client credentials scoped to a hotel chain or instance. A vendor starts with a ticket in the Stayntouch help center, returns the API Client Certification form, signs an NDA and agreements, and then gets sandbox access. After certification Stayntouch activates the integration in production.
systems.sandbox: Sandbox (UAT) access after the agreements are signed.
systems.limits: Not published. Confirm with Stayntouch.
blockers: Stayntouch reviews the certification for correctness, stability and data security before activating production, and publishes no timeline or fee. Confirm them with Stayntouch.
Each property must email Stayntouch to authorize your access to its production data.
systems.request: Your Stayntouch certification status, the property’s authorization email to Stayntouch, the chain or instance your credentials cover, and the room types and rates the agent may book.
systems.check: Reservations and guest requests land in Stayntouch on the right property, room type and rate, with no duplicate guest.

risk.title: Stayntouch certifies and activates each integration
risk.detail: Production access comes only after Stayntouch reviews your certification and the property authorizes you by email, and neither step has a published timeline.
risk.mitigation: Open the integration ticket and send the certification form in week 1, and have the property send its authorization email on day 1. Until activation, staff confirm the agent’s bookings in Stayntouch.

systems.name: Accela Civic Platform
systems.access: Accela Construct API (REST v4). Register an agency app (for staff users) on the Accela Developer Portal to get an App ID and secret; since August 2026 new developer accounts stay disabled until Accela approves the request. Tokens come from OAuth 2.0 (authorization code, implicit or password flow) and carry the agency name, the environment (such as TEST or PROD) and scopes. The agency’s administrator must enable your app for the agency in the Construct Admin Portal, and Accela support (hosted) or the agency’s Construct admin (on-premises) gives you the agency and environment names.
systems.sandbox: The Developer Portal’s Test API Token utility issues tokens against Accela’s shared test agency (the docs name Islandton; a 2017 release note says to use NULLISLAND for clean data). It holds demo data, not the agency’s record types or fees, so replay in the agency’s own TEST environment once its admin enables your app there.
systems.limits: Per-app rate limits are set by the agency in the Agency Admin Portal and enforced since June 2026: over the limit returns 429 with X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset headers. Accela publishes no numbers and may also throttle traffic it sees as degrading the API. Access tokens last 15 minutes and refresh tokens 8 hours. Confirm the agency’s limit with Accela.
blockers: Accela’s Developer Terms of Use bar collecting fees for an app from third parties unless an agreement with Accela authorizes it, so a paid agent needs an Accela agreement. Accela publishes no partner criteria, timeline or fee; confirm them with Accela.
The agency’s Construct admin must enable your app for the agency, and must tick Payment Enabled separately before the app can call the Commit Payment API.

Accela’s standard subscription agreement defines an Authorized User as a named employee, contractor or agent the customer bought a subscription for, so the agent’s staff login may need its own licensed seat. Confirm with the agency.

Refresh tokens expire after 8 hours, so an unattended agent needs a re-authorization plan. Construct admins can generate and revoke refresh tokens per app in the Admin Portal; confirm the approach with Accela.
systems.request: The agency name and its TEST and PROD environment names, the Construct admin enabling your App ID with the scopes you need, a dedicated Civic Platform user for the agent, the per-app rate limit the agency set, the modules and record types in scope, and Accela’s written authorization for commercial use.
systems.check: Records the agent creates in the agency’s TEST environment land with the right record type, address and parcel, contacts and fees, workflow starts at the expected task, and no call returns 429 at the agency’s configured limit.

risk.title: Accela must authorize a paid third-party app
risk.detail: Accela’s Developer Terms of Use forbid collecting fees for an app from third parties without an agreement with Accela, and the app still does nothing for an agency until that agency’s admin enables it.
risk.mitigation: Contact Accela’s partner team in week 1 for a written agreement that covers your use, and get the agency admin to enable your app in TEST. Until both exist, the agent drafts applications that staff enter in Accela.

systems.name: Tyler EnerGov (Enterprise Permitting & Licensing)
systems.access: Tyler sells the EnerGov (now Enterprise Permitting & Licensing, EPL) APIs as licensed toolkits on the agency’s Tyler contract, such as the Community Development API Toolkit and the Business Management API Toolkit. Tyler provides each toolkit’s documentation on request, and buying one includes no Tyler development work. Tyler publishes no EPL developer portal or self-serve keys (checked November 2026), so credentials come from the agency’s EPL environment once the toolkit is licensed. Civic Access is Tyler’s applicant portal, not an integration API.
systems.sandbox: Not published. Tyler’s implementation plans set up a testing environment per agency, so confirm with the agency and Tyler that a non-production EPL environment exists and that the API toolkit works there too.
systems.limits: Not published. Confirm with Tyler.
blockers: The API toolkit is a separate annual line item. Indio, California’s 2021 Tyler amendment listed the EnerGov Community Development API Toolkit at $9,534 a year before discount. Pricing varies by contract, so confirm the agency owns the toolkit.
EPL suites are licensed per named user in Tyler contracts such as Indio’s, so the agent’s login may need its own seat. Confirm the user count with the agency.
Confirm the agency’s EPL version. One integrator’s guide (SeeClickFix) requires EPL 9.6.1 or later for the REST/JSON API and warns that the API license may cost extra.

Tyler publishes no developer program for outside EPL vendors. Partner inquiries go through Tyler’s Connect With Tyler form, and the Tyler Platform Alliance covers Tyler’s Application Platform and Data & Insights, not EPL. Confirm the path with Tyler.
systems.request: Whether the agency’s Tyler investment summary includes the EPL API toolkits (Community Development, Business Management), the toolkit documentation from Tyler, the EPL version and hosting (Tyler-hosted or on-premises), API credentials and a named user for the agent in a test environment, and the permit, license and case types in scope.
systems.check: Permit applications and inspection requests the agent creates through the toolkit in the test environment land on the right parcel and contact with the expected fees and workflow step, and nothing posts to production.

risk.title: The agency may not own the EPL API toolkit
risk.detail: Tyler licenses EPL APIs as paid toolkits on the agency’s contract and publishes no self-serve keys or developer program for outside vendors. If the toolkit isn’t on the contract, adding it is a Tyler order that goes through the agency’s procurement.
risk.mitigation: On the first call, ask for the Tyler investment summary and look for the API toolkit lines. If they’re missing, request the Tyler quote in week 1 and launch with drafts that staff enter in EPL.

systems.name: Desktop or on-premises app (no API)
systems.access: Screen automation on a dedicated machine or VM, or read access to the app’s database if the vendor allows it.
systems.sandbox: Rarely. Ask for a training or test copy of the app.
systems.limits: Bound by how fast the UI responds; one session per machine.
blockers: Needs a dedicated machine, remote access, and its own login with MFA handled.
Any UI update can break the automation.
The vendor’s terms may restrict automation or database access.
systems.request: A dedicated machine or VM, a service login, and notice of the vendor’s update schedule.
systems.check: Every step confirms the screen it expects before it types or clicks.

risk.title: A vendor update breaks screen automation
risk.detail: UI changes in the legacy app silently break the steps the agent relies on.
risk.mitigation: Check each screen before acting, alert on mismatch, and fall back to staff.

systems.name: SFTP or CSV exports
systems.access: Scheduled file drops over SFTP, or exports someone runs by hand.
systems.sandbox: Sample files from the customer.
systems.limits: Data is only as fresh as the last export.
blockers: Column names and formats change without notice.
Someone must own the export schedule.
systems.request: SFTP credentials, three recent sample files, and the export schedule and owner.
systems.check: Each file is validated against the expected columns before anything is loaded.

risk.title: The agent acts on stale data
risk.detail: Between exports, the agent can tell people things that are no longer true.
risk.mitigation: Show data age in the agent’s context and avoid promises that depend on fresh data.

systems.name: Payer, carrier or vendor web portal
systems.access: Browser automation against a web portal under the customer’s credentials.
systems.sandbox: None. Dry-run each step against real pages without submitting.
systems.limits: Session timeouts, CAPTCHAs and account lockouts.
blockers: MFA on the portal login must be handled with the customer.
The portal’s terms may prohibit automation. Some insurance carriers’ terms ban bots and AI tools without written permission.
Portal layouts change without notice.
systems.request: A dedicated portal login, the MFA method, and confirmation that automation is allowed.
systems.check: Each portal step verifies the page before it reads or submits.

risk.title: Portal locks the account or changes layout
risk.detail: Automated logins can trigger lockouts, and layout changes break steps without warning.
risk.mitigation: Use a dedicated login, slow the request rate, and fall back to staff on any mismatch.

systems.name: Fax or email intake
systems.access: An e-fax service’s API or a shared mailbox; documents need OCR and extraction.
systems.sandbox: A sample set of past documents.
systems.limits: Extraction quality depends on scan quality and handwriting.
blockers: Documents often contain PHI or PII; storage and retention need agreement.
Forms vary by sender.
systems.request: Access to the fax service or mailbox and a few hundred past documents with their final outcome.
systems.check: Extracted fields match what staff entered for the same documents.

risk.title: Extraction errors on poor scans
risk.detail: Handwritten or low-quality documents produce confident but wrong fields.
risk.mitigation: Send low-confidence fields to staff review instead of writing them.

systems.name: Custom in-house system
systems.access: Whatever the customer’s engineers expose: an internal API, a database view, or a new endpoint they build.
systems.sandbox: Depends on the customer’s engineering team.
systems.limits: Unknown until their team documents them.
blockers: The customer’s engineers must prioritize the work.
Documentation is often missing or out of date.
systems.request: A named engineer on their side, API docs or a schema, and a test environment.
systems.check: Every call is checked against the customer engineer’s documented contract.

risk.title: Their engineers have other priorities
risk.detail: If the customer must build or change an endpoint, your launch waits on their roadmap.
risk.mitigation: Agree on the exact endpoint and a date in week 1, or design around a read-only path.

agents.label: Back-office / ops
agents.history: completed work items (tickets, forms, records) with their final outcome

agents.label: Other
agents.history: past interactions with their final outcome

fallbacks.label: Human team
fallbacks.killSwitch: Set agent traffic to 0%. New {units} go to the customer’s human team.
fallbacks.handoff: Warm handoff to the human team with a summary of what the agent already collected.

risks.title: The human team isn’t ready for handoffs
risks.detail: Staff who weren’t briefed get transfers with no context or at hours nobody covers.
risks.mitigation: Brief the team before shadow mode and test handoffs at every covered hour.

fallbacks.label: Voicemail
fallbacks.killSwitch: Set agent traffic to 0%. New {units} go to voicemail and a named owner works the callback queue.
fallbacks.handoff: Send the person to voicemail or a message form, and log a callback task with the agent’s summary.

risks.title: Failures turn into a callback backlog
risks.detail: When the agent hands off to voicemail, every failure becomes a callback someone has to make.
risks.mitigation: Name a callback owner and a same-day target before the 10% stage.

fallbacks.label: None
fallbacks.route: a fallback that must be set up first
fallbacks.killSwitch: Set agent traffic to 0%. Until a fallback exists, new {units} have nowhere to go.
fallbacks.handoff: Set up a fallback before any live traffic: a staffed queue, an on-call person or a callback list.

risks.title: The kill switch has nowhere to send people
risks.detail: With no fallback today, stopping the agent means dropping {units}.
risks.mitigation: Set up a staffed queue or callback list before the 10% stage. Don’t start live traffic without it.

timeline.paper: Name an owner on each side for the security review and the DPA, and for every BAA if health data is in scope.

stages.label: Shadow
stages.what: The agent sees real {units} and drafts its actions. Nothing is written and nobody hears from it. Staff compare its drafts with what they did.
stages.exit: Agreed checks pass on shadow traffic and staff sign off on the failures.

stages.what: One in ten {units} goes to the agent. The rest follow today’s route.
stages.exit: No unsafe writes, escalations within the agreed range, and every failure reviewed.

stages.what: Half of {units} go to the agent, including peak hours.
stages.exit: The same checks hold at peak volume and the fallback team keeps up.

stages.what: All {units} go to the agent. The fallback and kill switch stay in place.
stages.exit: Replay checks rerun whenever a connected system changes.

triggers: Any write to the wrong record or account.
Escalation or error rate above the threshold agreed with the customer.
A connected system starts failing or changes its fields.
Customer staff report a problem they can’t work around.
